Body:
The fix in #32088 only triggers session recovery on HTTP **404** (`Session not found`). However, not all MCP servers signal an expired session with 404.

The Atlassian/Jira MCP server (server: `uvicorn`, `Atlassian MCP v1.12.4`) used in our enterprise setup responds with **HTTP 400** when the session has expired. Reproduced against the live server by sending a `POST tools/list` with a stale `mcp-session-id`:

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
server: uvicorn
content-length: 41

Bad Request: No valid session ID provided
```

And the initial handshake (no session yet) returns a structured JSON-RPC error:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"server-error","error":{"code":-32600,"message":"Bad Request: Missing session ID"}}
```

Because the recovery logic only reinitializes on 404, our sessions never auto-recover: after the server-side idle timeout, every subsequent tool call fails with `Bad Request: No valid session ID provided` until opencode is fully restarted. This happens reliably every ~15-30 min of inactivity.

Would it be possible to extend the recovery trigger to also cover a **400** carrying a session-id error — e.g. response body containing `No valid session ID` / `Missing session ID`, or JSON-RPC code `-32600` with `session` in the message? That would make the recovery work for spec-compliant-ish servers that use 400 instead of 404 for expired/missing sessions.

Environment:
- opencode 1.17.8 (desktop, macOS)
- MCP transport: remote Streamable HTTP (`type: remote`)
- Server: Atlassian MCP 1.12.4 (uvicorn)

A strong +1 from a **multi-model independent sampling / review convergence** use case: the important part for us is being able to have one orchestrator delegate the **same role/prompt** to different models in the same run, then compare agreement/disagreement and converge on the result.

That is useful for review-consensus and second-opinion loops, and it breaks down if we have to duplicate agent definitions per model. We want agents to stay **role-centric**, with the caller choosing the model **per invocation** when needed.

So this feels directly aligned with **#17595** and **#29984**, and it would also help unblock downstream review flows like **#30289**. Not asking for a separate fallback mechanism here — just first-class runtime model selection for Task/subagent calls.

I can reproduce a closely related failure on OpenCode 1.17.8 / Bun 1.3.14 in a Linux dev container.

In my case, plain `opencode` black-screens / crashes when run inside a Git repo under `/workspaces`, while this works:

```bash
OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER=true opencode
```

A few useful details:

* `opencode run "hello"` works, so the model/agent path is fine.
* A non-Git directory under `/workspaces` works.
* An empty Git repo under `/workspaces` crashes.
* A fake Git env also works: `GIT_DIR=/tmp/no-git-dir GIT_WORK_TREE=/tmp/no-git-work-tree opencode`
* Watcher usage was not near kernel limits during testing (roughly 7k–13k watches, 5 inotify instances; limits 65,536 / 128), so this is not only active global inotify exhaustion.
* The crash signature is exit code 132 (SIGILL), Bun panic: `Segmentation fault at address 0x0`.

I’d like to submit a fix: watcher initialization should not block or kill TUI startup. If watcher setup fails, OpenCode should log a warning, disable the watcher, and continue running.
This is a rather serious problem; it will affect the use of ACP.

@rekram1-node my use-case:
- Orchestrator primary agent has edit: deny and has task permission allow for "Developer" subagent
- Orchestrator starts a subagent, eg Developer
- Developer has edit: allow

With current version of opencode Developer cannot use edit/write tool because he inherits Orchestrator deny.
eg. His own edit permission does not overwrite the permission from Orchestrator. 

Now I could set Orchestrator to edit: allow, however now I risk that if he forgets his primary instruction to not edit/write files on his own, he WILL start doing it by mistake. 

**Also a side note if i recall correctly, other use-cases:**
Orchestrator -> Lead dev -> dev
edit deny -> edit allow -> edit allow

Here dev can use write/edit tool. Because the bug seems to only affect forced permission from direct parent only.

Because lead dev has in leadDev.md edit permission: allow
dev can now edit/write files as the bug is not triggering in this use-case. 

Another use-case:
Orchestrator -> LeadDev -> Dev
edit: allow -> edit: deny -> edit allow

Here dev cannot use write/edit tool either. 

I don't understand how this can be intentional. 
You have the "Task" permission to allow or not allow using a subagent.
This subagent has his own permissions, respect them.

> I'd like to take this on. Here's my approach:
> 
> **How it works:**
> 
> * User sets `model: "auto"` in config (or types `auto` interactively)
> * A small classifier model (default `opencode/gpt-5-nano`, free) looks at the prompt and returns a complexity + task type score
> * A local routing function picks the best model from the available catalog or from a user-defined `model_pool` if they want to constrain choices
> * The classifier model is configurable, so users can swap in Ollama or any provider for offline use
> 
> **Config surface:**
> 
> "auto_model": {
>   "classifier_model": "opencode/gpt-5-nano",  // can be ollama/llama3.2:3b etc
>   "model_pool": ["anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5", "openai/gpt-5.2-codex"],  // optional constraint
>   "preferred_provider": "cheap"  // cheap | fast | capable
> }
> Happy to start small and iterate based on feedback. Would a PR along these lines be welcome?

Superseded by #32850 — same root cause, but the new issue adds the key finding that opencode-linux-x64-baseline works perfectly on the exact same CPU (VMware Ubuntu), proving this is a macOS-specific JIT issue rather than a fundamental CPU incompatibility.
Superseded by #32850 — same root cause, with new diagnostic evidence that Linux baseline works on the same hardware.

This supersedes my earlier reports #26877 and #26878. Those identified the SIGILL crash but assumed a fundamental CPU incompatibility. The new evidence: Linux baseline binary (same BuildID) works on the same physical CPU — proving the runtime can handle missing AVX2. The fix is not a new build target, but aligning macOS JIT behavior with Linux. Closing the earlier issues to consolidate discussion here.

Important update: The problem may not require a new build target — the Linux baseline binary already works on the same CPU.

I tested this on an Intel Xeon E5-1680 v2 (Ivy Bridge, no AVX2) — same crash on macOS, exact same SIGILL. But then in a VMware Ubuntu VM on the same physical machine, `opencode-linux-x64-baseline --version` outputs `1.17.8` without any crash.

Both binaries share the same BuildID (`c30f169b...`), embedding the same Bun/JavaScriptCore runtime. The difference: Linux baseline's JSC FTL JIT does runtime cpuid detection and falls back to SSE4.2/AVX1 when AVX2 is absent. macOS baseline's JIT hardcodes AVX2.

The fix: align macOS baseline JIT behavior with Linux — add runtime CPU feature fallback, not a new build target.
Consolidating into #29039 which tracks the exact same issue. The key new finding (Linux baseline works, fix is JIT behavior not a new build target) has been posted there.
